This is the year 2026. One might have hoped that, after thousands of years of war, humanity could have come up with a better way to resolve conflicts than killing and mass destruction. Unfortunately, that is not the case.  There is now more war and bloodshed raging across the world than at almost any point in decades. In February 2022, Vladimir Putin, without provocation, invaded Ukraine. The result: hundreds of thousands of soldiers and civilians killed, millions displaced and a war that grinds on with no end in sight. In October 2023, Hamas attacked Israel, killing 1,200 innocent people and taking 251 hostages. In response, Netanyahu and the Israeli military did not simply wage war against Hamas — they waged war against the entire population of Gaza. At least 73,000 Palestinians have been killed, the real toll almost certainly far higher, most of them women, children and the elderly. Virtually the entire physical infrastructure of Gaza has been destroyed. I agree with the major human rights organizations around the world who call this a genocide. Four months ago, in collusion with Netanyahu, Trump took a page from Putin's playbook: he started a war with Iran without provocation. The result of this war (and the ensuing Israeli war against Lebanon): 13 U.S. service members dead, thousands of Iranian and Lebanese civilians killed and more than $100 billion in U.S. taxpayer dollars spent. And in the midst of all of this — Ukraine, Gaza, Iran — there is another horrific war happening now that is getting relatively little attention: the civil war and genocide in Sudan. Sudan's two rival military factions, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), the country's national army, and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary group, have been at war since 2023. The RSF descends from the Janjaweed militias that carried out Sudan's first genocide in Darfur two decades ago, killing as many as 400,000 non-Arab civilians. Today, the RSF is trying to finish what it started. The State Department has formally determined that the RSF is committing genocide, again, murdering men and boys and systematically raping women and girls because of their ethnicity. Last October, the RSF laid siege to the city of El-Fasher; in just the first three days after it fell, an estimated 6,000 people were killed. Right now, the same horror is unfolding in the city of El-Obeid, where nearly half a million people are trapped. Let’s be clear. Trump’s good friend and staunch U.S. ally, the United Arab Emirates dictatorship, run by one of the wealthiest families in the world — has financed and enabled this genocide for years. And why is this happening? Billions of dollars of looted gold from Sudan is flowing straight into the pockets of Emirati oligarchs – making a multibillionaire family even richer. This has been documented by the United Nations, independent journalists, and international human rights organizations. Here is the scale of what this war has caused: at least 59,000 people confirmed killed since 2023, with credible estimates running as high as 150,000. Fourteen million people driven from their homes. Thirty million people, two–thirds of Sudan's population, in need of emergency humanitarian assistance just to survive. U.S. foreign policy must be based on a respect for democracy and human rights. We cannot be complicit in the face of genocide, no matter where it is happening. Congress must demand that the UAE cease its military support for the RSF and work with the international community and the Sudanese people to bring an end to this horrific conflict and provide the humanitarian aid that is desperately needed there.

This week, Representative Darren Soto and I introduced the “Federal Investment Restrictions on Equipment from Worrisome Authoritarian Linked Locations (FIREWALL) Act. This bipartisan legislation is designed to safeguard America's telecommunications infrastructure from foreign adversaries by prohibiting federal telecommunications funding from being used to purchase fiber-optic cable sourced from countries of concern. The legislation builds upon ongoing efforts to secure U.S. communications networks from foreign threats and prevent hostile regimes from gaining access to critical American infrastructure. America's telecommunications networks are the backbone of our economy, our national security, and our daily lives. As our adversaries become increasingly sophisticated in their efforts to infiltrate critical infrastructure, we must act proactively to protect our communications systems from potential vulnerabilities. The FIREWALL Actensures that taxpayer dollars are not used to subsidize technology sourced from countries that pose a threat to our national security. Rather than waiting until these products are deeply embedded in our networks and facing another costly 'rip and replace' effort, we should take commonsense steps now to prevent the problem from occurring in the first place.

B000490.text: This week, the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, appeared before the U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government. During the hearing, I asked the Director about how Congress can be any clearer to ensure that the Trump Administration understands that once a funding bill is signed into law, the President is not allowed to change or second-guess the spending and withhold it due to policy or political differences. That is at the heart of Article 1 of the U.S. Constitution and why Congress also passed the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, when President Nixon tried to withhold funds that were already obligated according to the law.

This week, I asked the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, to explain how poorly planned cuts to the federal workforce last year have weakened services and protections upon which Americans rely. This includes the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, which is responsible for protecting America’s agriculture from invasive species and diseases. USDA-APHIS began mounting a vigorous response to the resurgence of New World Screwworm – a deadly parasite affecting livestock – in 2024. However, in early 2025, the Administration illegally fired workers and forced others to resign, causing over 25 percent of all USDA-APHIS employees to leave. USDA’s New World Screwworm prevention, monitoring, surveillance, and control efforts were halted. USDA had approved $378 million in prevention and control funding for sterile fly facilities in 2023 and 2024, yet the money went unspent when the new administration paused funding. This is extremely concerning to our ranchers, and this outbreak could drive the price of food even higher. Unfortunately, we continue to see the fallout of the blunt and ill-considered cuts to federal workers, from the return of New World Screwworm to the United States, to farmers showing up to closed or understaffed Farm Service Agency offices, to attacks on our nuclear safety programs putting national security at risk. I will continue to hold the White House accountable, as I did this week during the U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government hearing with Mr. Vought.

Today, Congressman Austin Scott (GA-08) and I testified before the U.S. House Natural Resources Subcommittee on Federal Lands regarding our bipartisan bill, the Ocmulgee Mounds National Park Redesignation Act (H.R. 9416). As our nation prepares to celebrate its 250th birthday this Saturday, it is vital that we preserve and protect our ancient history, including the stories of the indigenous peoples who lived here long before July 4, 1776. Our bill today represents a small, albeit meaningful, step forward that will strengthen Ocmulgee and ensure that its cultural and religious sites are protected now and into the future. This continues a more than decade long, but steady and combined effort of local, state, and federal leaders to create Georgia’s first National Park and more closely realize the original vision for this historic and cultural treasure which will also bring more visitors and jobs to Middle Georgia.

Terrorists. Cartels. Human traffickers. Drug smugglers. Each day, ICE and Border Patrol agents and officers confront these threats head-on to keep America safe. It’s exactly why I have consistently voted to comprehensively resource these law enforcement professionals as they carry out their security missions. While the far-left hoped to eradicate funding for critical operations and weaken our border security apparatus, House Republicans have made clear that we will continue to support those who defend our homeland and keep our communities safe. That's why we passed the Secure America Act today. However, while I do not regret the objective of our actions today, I am appalled by the complete failure of Senate Democrats that led us to this moment. Chuck Schumer and his radical caucus twice shut down the government, instigating chaos across the nation. Since then, they have continued to diminish Article I and forced the use of reconciliation. It’s wrong – and deliberately undermines the appropriations process. The Constitution entrusts Congress with the power of the purse. Yet, in great irony, the Senate has shown greater concern for protecting an internal rule than fulfilling its constitutional duty. The filibuster is nothing more than an institutional habit. It is neither mentioned nor sanctioned in our founding documents. I would remind my peers on the other side of the Rotunda that no chamber precedent is greater than the bedrock of our Republic. Members swear an oath to uphold the Constitution – not the filibuster. I thoroughly regret the erosion of Article I authority that Senate Democrats have instigated, and the price everyday Americans have been forced to pay as a result. I hope the months-long charade that led us to this moment serves as a reminder that no partisan fixation is worth shutting down the government, abandoning constitutional responsibilities, and forcing Congress into extraordinary measures simply to perform its most basic duties. I believe in the Constitution, the power of the purse, and completing the appropriations process. I also believe in keeping the homeland safe. The Senate may have abandoned proper governing, but I will not abandon those who stand watch over our borders and protect our communities. Our work, of course, doesn’t end here. As the Fiscal Year 2027 Appropriations markups near completion, I am reminded that governing is a choice. The work I do, the votes I cast, and the actions I take will always be guided by one principle: fulfilling our obligations to the American people

This afternoon, while in Duval County alongside County Judge Arnold Cantu, County Sheriff Romeo Ramirez, County Clerk Sally Lichtenberger, and the Commissioners' Court, I announced $170,000 in federal funding I secured through the FY2025 Operation Stonegarden Grant Program for the Duval County Sheriff's Office. I helped create Operation Stonegarden because I knew our border communities needed a reliable federal partnership to support local law enforcement. Since Duval County joined the program in 2018, it has received more than $1.4 million to help cover personnel, equipment, supplies, and other operational costs. These federal dollars will help fund overtime for deputies, expand law enforcement coverage, strengthen public safety across Duval County, and ensure local officers have the resources they need to continue protecting our communities.

Today, alongside Zapata County Judge Joe Rathmell, Justice of the Peace Olga Bruni, Zapata County Sheriff Ramon Montes, and Commissioner Joey Solis, I announced $293,070 in federal funding I secured through the FY2025 Operation Stonegarden Grant Program for the Zapata County Sheriff's Office. As the original author of Operation Stonegarden, I've continued fighting to ensure our border communities have the resources they need to keep families safe. Since the program's creation, Zapata County has received more than $10.3 million through Operation Stonegarden to support local law enforcement. This funding will support overtime for local deputies, strengthen law enforcement efforts, enhance public safety across Zapata County, and allow the Sheriff's Office to purchase brand-new patrol units, helping improve emergency response capabilities throughout the county.

This morning, I announced $25 million in federal dollars I secured through the U.S. Department of Transportation's BUILD Grant Program for the City of Laredo's World Trade Bridge Expansion Project. This investment will help add two new lanes to the existing bridge and construct a new eight-lane northbound commercial bridge, increasing capacity, reducing congestion, and keeping goods moving more efficiently through our nation's busiest commercial port of entry. Today's announcement builds on my continued efforts to secure federal investments for Laredo's international bridges. In addition to this $25 million BUILD Grant, I've helped secure a $62 million renovation project for Bridge II and a $27 million renovation project for Bridge I in 2015, ensuring our ports of entry remain competitive and prepared for continued growth. Thank you to Mayor Dr. Victor Treviño, the City of Laredo, and all of our partners who helped make this project possible. I'll continue working to bring federal investments home and ensure South Texas has the infrastructure it needs to support jobs, strengthen our supply chain, and keep American trade moving. Together, we're continuing to strengthen Laredo's position as the nation's #1 inland port.

For 250 years, our great experiment has faltered, flourished, evolved, and progressed. The American experience is ever-changing and as diverse as the people who call this country home. But one thing has remained constant – the idea of America has always been a beacon of hope. Protecting this country and the ideals and values it was founded on takes work. Democracy is demanding. It takes dedication and principle. And it takes the resounding belief that upholding those ideals and values is worth the fight because America is bigger than any one person. Because liberty can only truly endure when it is paired with responsibility, virtue, and a commitment to put public good ahead of personal ambition. Today, we celebrate the moment when our founding fathers openly declared that creating this country, based in liberty, was a necessity in the face of tyranny. Their legacy is that leadership requires courage when it’s difficult, integrity when no one is watching, and a willingness to put country above self. We must remember that our duty is not merely to the next election, but to the next generation. That should be the challenge for all Americans as we look forward to another 250 years. From Massachusetts, where the fight for freedom first began, I wish you a happy 4th of July. God Bless America always, God Bless all who call her home, and God Bless our courageous men and women in uniform who continue the fight for liberty today.

On Monday, our office suffered an unimaginable loss. Chris Matthews, my District Outreach and Communications Director, passed away unexpectedly. If any one of you begin to lose faith in our country, remember Chris Matthews. Remember he was without question one of the Commonwealth’s sharpest political minds – a generational talent. Remember that he was more than a Congressional aide. He took the belief that through our actions we all can bring needed change and brought it with him on many interstate bus rides to canvas distant pivotal states and to the doors of the families he inspired. Remember through his example that public service is a genuinely noble vocation. As a trusted member of our office, he helped countless veterans, families, and those who could not advocate for themselves. Those of us privileged to have worked with him for over fifteen years will remember his laugh and his wry, often biting, humor – contrasting the way things are to the way they could be. We will always remember his authentic belief that in this country, people can bring about progress and meaningful change. It was real to him and his sincerity shown through. Chris was a genuinely good person. He was family to all of us, and we are devastated by his loss, particularly at such a young age. Our thoughts and prayers are with Molly and Eli and the many who loved him. Though we wish we had more time with him, his memory will continue to give us faith that one person can significantly make better the lives of those around him.

In Alaska, voting is not as simple as driving down the road to a neighborhood polling place. Many Alaskans live in remote communities that are not connected to the road system, requiring ballots to travel by bush plane or boat, which means volatile weather conditions and limited infrastructure can determine whether those ballots arrive on time. Today’s decision affirms that states have the flexibility to account for these realities and helps ensure that every American who lawfully casts a ballot has the opportunity to have it counted. https://apnews.com/article/supreme-court-mailed-ballots-trump-elections-5f24f718ea92a33838485ce6302e079e

Arkansas, and the United States, have an incredibly abundant source of timber. Unfortunately, we look to nations outside of our borders to supply us with a resource that we have right here in our own back yard. Healthy forest management is more than just taking care of our trees, in fact we have been loving our trees to death. Our forests are overstocked and unhealthy because we have no markets for the wood and rural communities are suffering because their resource and economic opportunity are tied directly to the forests. A nation with such an abundance of timber should never be reliant on other countries to import lumber and pulp products, but that’s where we find ourselves.  Recently, we’ve seen paper mills across the country closing – even a few here in the Fourth District. With a background in Forestry and Engineering, Congressman Westerman understands just how important our pulp and paper industry is and he remains heavily focused on legislation that will support such an important economic contributer for Arkansas. This week’s meeting with the Pulp & Paperworkers’ Resource Council to discuss just how important the forest products industry underscored the need for Congress to work diligently to provide its support.

S001198.text: For Alaskans, the decades-long King Cove Road impasse has been a symbol of an uncaring, out-of-touch, faraway federal government that prioritizes the lives of birds over people. I’ve been working with the people of King Cove on this issue back to my time as Alaska’s Commissioner of the Department of Natural Resources through my time serving as U.S. Senator. Time and again these great Alaskans have kept hope alive, despite setbacks, most recently when the Biden administration disregarded the voices of the community and withdrew the previously approved land exchange. The permit issued by the Corps of Engineers today is vindication for King Cove, putting us closer than ever before to delivering a lifesaving, 11-mile, single-lane gravel road to the all-weather airport in Cold Bay. I want to thank the Administration, especially Secretary Burgum and Assistant Secretary of the Army for Civil Works Telle, for listening to Alaskans, for caring about their safety and well-being, and for putting us on the cusp of a historic breakthrough for safe and reliable access for King Cove.

First steel was being cut on our new Arctic Security Cutter months before the contract was even finalized! That’s the kind of initiative and urgency we need to build these new icebreakers and close the gap we face with our adversaries in the Arctic. With three of these new icebreakers being homeported right here in Alaska—in addition to the Storis in Juneau—we’re building a strong foundation for America’s Arctic Security future!

Last week, at the Port of Alaska groundbreaking ceremony, I mentioned the pressure my team and I have put on federal agency heads to resolve a decade-long lawsuit over port funding. Yesterday, a settlement was finally announced, unlocking $191 million to go directly toward construction and building on the hundreds of millions of federal dollars my congressional delegation colleagues and I have secured for the project over the years. The funding we’ve secured for the port is critically important for Alaska, first, because it will lower the cost of living for Alaska’s hard-working families—everything from energy to groceries. The port modernization is also vital for supporting the renaissance of energy development happening on the North Slope and the future build-out of the Alaska LNG project. Finally, the Port of Alaska is very important to U.S. national security and the military build-up taking place in our state, especially the historic $7 billion ‘Fighter Town’ recapitalization coming to JBER. I will continue pressing for the funding needed to complete this project and bringing up top federal officials—like the U.S. Attorney General, the U.S. Transportation Secretary, the MARAD Administrator, and the USTRANSCOM Commander—so they understand and appreciate how important this piece of infrastructure is for Alaska and for America.

During my tenure in the Senate, I have worked to secure historic levels of federal infrastructure investments for Alaska—funding that will help improve roads, bridges, ports, airports, and other crucial projects to our great state. But funding alone does not build projects. Bridging the gap between federal funding and actual project delivery—getting projects designed, approved, bid on, and under construction so that Alaskans can get to work—is just as important as securing these investments.   Last week, I joined @USDOTFHWA Sean McMaster and union leaders representing thousands of Alaskans for a roundtable on delivering federally funded transportation projects, strengthening workforce development, expanding apprenticeship opportunities, and ensuring these investments create jobs for Alaskans and move projects forward.   I will always fight to ensure infrastructure investments in Alaska become a reality and benefit Alaskans.

K000391.text: As America begins its 250th anniversary year, I'm excited to share the Schaumburg Township Historical Society's contribution to my office's America250 Time Capsule Project. Thank you to the Schaumburg Township Historical Society for helping preserve the history that makes our communities unique.

As America begins its 250th anniversary year, I'm excited to share Des Plaines' contribution to my office's America250 Time Capsule Project. Des Plaines chose a collection of postcards and photographs highlighting the places that have shaped the city's history—from Ray Kroc's first McDonald's franchise and the city's railroad heritage to the the Des Plaines Public Library, and the Des Plaines River. As one description explains, the first McDonald's franchise "would leap from a novel, local establishment to one of the largest restaurant chains in the world. Its enduring legacy reminds us of the city's nationally poignant history and innovative culture." Another notes that preserving the Des Plaines River and surrounding forest "show[s] the importance of nature to Des Plaines." Thank you to everyone who helped tell the story of Des Plaines through this thoughtful collection.

There are some people you are simply grateful to have known. Tom Yaegel of Richboro was one of them. He was a veteran, patriot, builder, mentor, and a man whose life touched far more people than he probably ever knew—a true Hometown Hero. I was proud to call him a friend, and will always remember his quick wit, larger-than-life presence, relentless drive, and the deep love he had for his family, community, and country. Tom answered America’s call during the Vietnam War, earning his commission through Officer Candidate School and serving in the Army Corps of Engineers in support of U.S. Special Forces. When he came home, he built a life with the same grit and determination he brought to his service. For 56 years, he shared that life with his beloved wife, Ann. He built a family he adored, businesses that became local institutions, and opportunities that changed lives. Through the Richboro Swim Club and Valley of Fear, Tom created more than places people visited. He created places people remember. Generations of families spent their summers there. Generations of young people got their first jobs there. Friendships began there. Traditions took root there. And so many people learned from Tom that hard work, responsibility, loyalty, and doing right by others still matter. That is the kind of legacy that lasts. As our great nation continues to mark 250 years, Tom’s life is a reminder that the strength of this country has always come from people like him—Americans who serve when called, create opportunity, invest and uplift others, and leave their communities stronger than they found them. Tom did all of that. May we keep Ann, his children, grandchildren, the entire Yaegel family, and all who knew and loved Tom in our prayers. Our community is better because of him, and his legacy will live on here forever.

For nearly a year and a half, we have worked side by side with the families of Upper Makefield and the Mt. Eyre Neighborhood Resident Task Force—at kitchen tables, on affected properties, with regulators, and at every stage of this fight. From day one, we have pushed for independent testing, a full operational shutdown, complete remediation, and accountability from Sunoco and every responsible agency. And when this crisis exposed failures that reached beyond Upper Makefield, we acted—working with the community to turn those lessons into the bipartisan Wojnovich Pipeline Safety Act. Tonight, we continued that work and put the next set of demands plainly on the record. Sunoco and PADEP must provide a full and unredacted accounting of this spill, clear answers on how much fuel remains underground, a credible remediation timeline, measurable standards for completion, and independent oversight throughout the cleanup. The progress made in this fight has come from sustained partnership, hard questions, and a community that refused to let up. That is how we have approached this from the beginning, and that is how we will continue—working together, pressing for answers, and seeing this through until Upper Makefield has the permanent solution it deserves. 🔗Read more: http://fitzpatrick.house.gov/2025/11/fitzpatrick-introduces-wojnovich-pipeline-safety-act-following-upper-makefield-jet-fuel-leak-and-months-of-federal-oversight

A000375.text: John Adams called Independence Day America’s “Day of Deliverance.” The Declaration of Independence - that sacred parchment - is the cornerstone of American exceptionalism and the foundation for the longest-sustained constitutional democracy in the world. It affirms the birthright of every American citizen: our God-given rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. The Declaration of Independence wasn’t just a list of grievances; it was a treatise on man and his natural rights - a mission statement for how such men should be governed. No one at the time gave us a fighting chance of defeating the world’s superpower for our independence. And few predicted we’d persist for a quarter of a millennium. Our founding visionaries weren’t sure of either outcome themselves, but they believed in our inherent rights and God-given freedoms and would rather die fighting for them than live under tyranny. They trusted in “divine Providence” for protection and mutually pledged to each other “our Lives, our Fortunes and our sacred Honor.” They held fast to truth, they stood firm for justice, and they fought like warrior poets for our freedom. And, by the grace of Almighty God, our revolutionary ancestors gave birth to the most powerful and prosperous nation in human history. Let’s honor their vision, courage, and conviction by solemnly dedicating ourselves to preserving this “Great Experiment” in liberty and self-government. Happy 250th Independence Day to all my God-fearing, freedom-loving American patriots! May God continue to have mercy upon and give favor to our beloved nation. U-S-A, U-S-A…!! Your proud US Representative and fellow West Texan, Jodey

Fun Fact Friday: As we celebrate the 250th anniversary of American independence, I want to highlight some of the signers of the Declaration of Independence. Thomas Lynch was born in South Carolina in 1749. He spent several years in England studying and meeting with many English politicians. Upon hearing about the unrest in the colonies, he traveled back to America. His father had been elected to serve in the Continental Congress, but his father’s health was failing. Therefore, Thomas came in and served alongside his father. Thomas signed the Declaration but his father’s health issues prevented him from signing the document before his death. Thomas and his wife passed away in 1779, when the ship he and his wife were traveling on disappeared into the Bermuda Triangle.

K000377.text: Just over one year ago, Trump and Republicans gave a tax break to rich people and paid for it by gutting Americans’ healthcare and food assistance. Arizona has been one of the hardest hit states. Nearly 2 million Arizonans, roughly 1 in 4, rely on Medicaid. In Arizona, it’s called AHCCCS. This program has helped seniors, kids, and families across our state afford the care they need. But because of Trump and Republicans, hundreds of thousands of Arizonans are expected to lose their healthcare in the coming years as Medicaid cuts take effect. That's not cutting waste, fraud, and abuse. That's taking healthcare away from people who need it at a time when costs are rising. We can already see the impact on food assistance programs. Arizona's SNAP enrollment is already down nearly 50% since last July. St. Mary's Food Bank is seeing 15% more demand. And in Flagstaff, 28% more people showed up for food assistance last month than the same time last year. These aren't just numbers. These are people. These are families who can’t afford to buy food and are showing up at food banks because Republicans cut their benefits to pay for a tax break for millionaires and billionaires. The promise of this country is that if you work hard, you can build a good life. That’s only getting harder because Republicans in Washington prioritize the rich over working Americans. But we don’t have to accept that. I won’t stop fighting until we fix it.

C001129.text: On this day in history, in 1804 in New Jersey, Aaron Burr mortally wounds Alexander Hamilton in a duel. Aaron Burr, who was the third Vice President at the time, and Alexander Hamilton, the first and previous Secretary of the Treasury, had a rivalry for many years. The duel was the result of Hamilton referring to Burr as a “dangerous man” in a published newspaper article. Although the witnesses turned around before shots were fired since duels were illegal in New Jersey, it’s believed that Hamilton shot into the air while Burr fired at Hamilton’s hip. Hamilton died the next day. Burr was charged with murder in New York and New Jersey, but his allies had the charges dropped. He finished out his term as Vice President, which marked the end of his political career.

On this day in history in 1985, France’s foreign intelligence agency bombed the Greenpeace flagship Rainbow Warrior in New Zealand’s Auckland Harbor. The ship was preparing to lead a protest against French nuclear testing in the Pacific when two French agents planted explosives onboard, killing a photographer. France initially denied involvement, but after the agents were captured, the government admitted responsibility.

On this day in history in 1795, James Swan paid off the entire U.S. national debt of $2,024,899. A Boston patriot and member of the Sons of Liberty, Swan bought the U.S. debt to France and sold it as interest-bearing shares to private investors. This move shifted America’s debt from foreign governments to private hands, strengthening the young nation’s financial footing.

On this day in history in 1950, General Douglas MacArthur was appointed commander of United Nations forces in Korea, just weeks after North Korea’s invasion. Known for leading successful campaigns in the Pacific during World War II, MacArthur initially turned the tide of the Korean War with a bold landing at Inchon. However, his later push into North Korea and public disagreements with President Truman led to his dismissal less than a year later. In his farewell statement to Congress, he famously said, "Old soldiers never die; they just fade away."

One year ago today, on the Fourth of July, our nation celebrated the blessings of freedom while families across Texas experienced unimaginable heartbreak. We pause today to remember every precious life lost at Camp Mystic and every other life taken far too soon in that tragedy. We remember the children whose futures were just beginning, the counselors and adults who stood courageously in harm’s way, and every family whose lives were forever changed. Their names, their stories, and their memories will never be forgotten. No words can truly ease the pain of such profound loss. Yet even in the darkest moments, we witnessed the very best of America. To every law enforcement officer, firefighter, EMS professional, dispatcher, game warden, pilot, medic, search-and-rescue specialist, and every first responder who answered the call, thank you. You ran toward danger while others were running away. You worked through exhaustion, heartbreak, and impossible conditions with courage, professionalism, and compassion. Your service honored every life you were fighting to save. To the countless volunteers who showed up without being asked—neighbors, veterans, church groups, ranchers, boat owners, businesses, families, and complete strangers—you reminded us that the strength of our communities is measured not only by what we say, but by what we do. You brought supplies, comfort, equipment, prayers, and hope. You asked for nothing in return except the opportunity to help another human being. That spirit defines Texas. As we remember those we lost, let us also remember the enduring responsibility we share: to love our neighbors, to care for those who grieve, and to ensure that the memories of these lives continue to inspire acts of kindness, service, and sacrifice. Finally, I want to offer my deepest gratitude to the men of the BEARKAT team. There are simply no words sufficient to express what you endured or what you accomplished. You answered a calling that demanded extraordinary courage, unwavering resolve, and selfless service. You carried burdens that few will ever fully understand, and you did so with quiet professionalism and humility. It is impossible to thank you enough for all that you did. Your actions brought comfort to grieving families, hope in moments of despair, and honor to everyone you represent. Texas will forever be grateful, and your service will never be forgotten. May we always remember those we lost, honor those who served, and carry forward the enduring truth that even in our darkest hours, courage, compassion, and faith will always light the way.
Happy Fourth of July, America. God bless 🇺🇸

On this day in 1944, over 34,000 American soldiers crowded together in small, amphibious boats en route to Omaha Beach. As the boats landed on the beach, and their bow ramps dropped down leading the men ashore, unrelenting machine gun fire rained down from enemy bunkers. Undeterred, the American and Allied forces emerged from the battle victorious, but not without a heavy cost. Over 2,500 Americans died at Omaha Beach. One of them was 1st Lieutenant Thomas Royce Dallas Jr. from our Congressional District in Griffin, Georgia, who drew his last breath on the shores of Omaha Beach. As we remember the heroism Americans exhibited on D-Day and we reflect on the cost of freedom, may we remember and be inspired by the names and faces of those brave soldiers who died in service to our Country.
